These operations\\nautomatically distribute processing across multiple AWS Regions to ensure reliable service\\ndelivery.\\n\\nThe following Automated Reasoning operations use cross-Region inference:\\n\\n* `StartAutomatedReasoningPolicyBuildWorkflow` \u2014 Invoked during policy\\n creation and compilation from source documents.\\n* `StartAutomatedReasoningPolicyTestWorkflow` \u2014 Invoked during policy\\n validation and testing procedures.\\n* Runtime validation \u2014 Invoked when a guardrail that includes an Automated Reasoning\\n policy checks content.\\n\\nThese operations use large language models. The models extract formal logic rules from\\nsource documents and translate natural language into logic that Automated Reasoning checks\\nagainst your policy. The following table shows where Automated Reasoning might\\nprocess a request, based on the Region where the request originates.\\n\\nWhere Automated Reasoning processes requests\\n\\n| Request originates in | Automated Reasoning might process the request in |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), US East (Ohio) | Any supported US Region |\\n| EU (Frankfurt), EU (Paris), EU (Ireland) | Any supported EU Region |\\n| Asia Pacific (Sydney) | Any supported Region in Australia |\\n\\n**Important:**\\n\\nCustomer data remains within the geographic boundary where the request originates\\n(the United States, the European Union, or Australia). AWS processes this data in\\naccordance with AWS data residency commitments.\\n\\nCross-Region inference operates transparently without requiring customer configuration.\\nAPI functionality remains consistent regardless of the specific Region that processes the\\nrequest.\\n\\n###### Topics\\n\\n* Automated Reasoning checks concepts\\n* Create your Automated Reasoning policy\\n* Automated Reasoning policy best practices\\n* Test an Automated Reasoning policy\\n* Troubleshoot and refine your Automated Reasoning policy\\n* Use Kiro CLI with an Automated Reasoning policy\\n* Deploy your Automated Reasoning policy in your application\\n* Integrate Automated Reasoning checks in your application\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-automated-reasoning-checks.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Api-Bedrock-2023-04-20\",\"context\":\"### GuardrailAutomatedReasoningPolicyConfig\\n\\n##### Description\\n\\nConfiguration settings for integrating Automated Reasoning policies with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.\\n\\n##### Members\\n\\n**confidenceThreshold**\\n: : **Type:** *double*\\n\\n The confidence threshold for triggering guardrail actions based on Automated Reasoning policy violations.\\n\\n**policies**\\n: : **Required**: *Yes*\\n : **Type:** *Array of strings*\\n\\n The list of Automated Reasoning policy ARNs to include in the guardrail configuration\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-sdk-php/v3/api/api-bedrock-2023-04-20.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"amazon-bedrock\",\"skill_description\":\"Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. For SageMaker model discovery, customization, or endpoints, use aws-ai-ml.\\n\\nServices: bedrock, bedrock-runtime, bedrock-mantle, bedrock-agent, bedrock-agent-runtime, bedrock-agentcore-control, bedrock-agentcore\\nTasks: deploy, debug, optimize, design, migrate\\nPersona: developer, devops, architect\\nWorkload: generative-ai, rag, agents\\n*\",\"skill_name\":\"amazon-bedrock\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Read Bedrock Automated Reasoning checks guardrail docs"}

{"id": "8c579230-9990-434a-aff9-9dfc6994b804", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_gu0AwUbnyc4xutXYeTbPiL", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-contextual-grounding-check.html\",\"content\":\"Table of Contents:\\n- Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses (char 0-20832)\\n  - Add contextual grounding checks with the console (char 8455-11353)\\n  - Configure contextual grounding checks with the API (char 11354-13848)\\n  - Calling contextual grounding check with Invoke APIs (char 13849-16115)\\n  - Calling contextual grounding check with Converse APIs (char 16116-18201)\\n  - Calling contextual grounding check with ApplyGuardrail API (char 18202-20832)\\n    - How qualifiers affect policy evaluation (char 19396-20832)\\n\\n# Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails supports contextual grounding checks to detect and filter hallucinations in model\\nresponses when a reference source and a user query is provided. The supported use cases\\ninclude summarization, paraphrasing, and question answering. Standard tier also supports\\nresponses that include reasoning or conversational content. Classic tier does not\\nsupport conversational use cases. For more information, see Safeguard tiers for contextual\\ngrounding checks on this page.\\n\\nContextual grounding checks check for relevance for each chunk processed. If any one\\nchunk is deemed relevant, the whole response is considered relevant as it has the answer\\nto user's query. For streaming API, this can result in scenario where an irrelevant\\nresponse is returned to the user and is only marked as irrelevant after the whole\\nresponse is streamed.\\n\\nContextual grounding checks the following paradigms:\\n\\n* **Grounding** \u2013 This checks if the model\\n  response is factually accurate based on the source and is grounded in the\\n  source. Any new information introduced in the response will be considered\\n  un-grounded.\\n* **Relevance** \u2013 This checks if the model\\n  response is relevant to the user query.\\n\\nConsider an example where the reference source contains \\\"London is the capital of UK.\\nTokyo is the capital of Japan\\\" and the user query is \\\"What is the capital of Japan?\\\". A\\nresponse such as \\\"The capital of Japan is London\\\" will be considered ungrounded and\\nfactually incorrect, where as a response such as \\\"The capital of UK is London\\\" will be\\nconsidered irrelevant, even if it's correct and grounded in the source.\\n\\n**Safeguard tiers for\\ncontextual grounding checks**\\n\\nContextual grounding checks support two safeguard\\ntiers. The tier determines how the check evaluates responses and which\\nlanguages it supports.\\n\\n**Classic tier** evaluates strict grounding. Any\\ninformation in the response that is not stated in the grounding source lowers the\\ngrounding score, including reasonable inferences and conversational phrasing. Classic\\ntier supports English, French, and Spanish.\\n\\n**Standard tier** provides a more robust solution than\\nClassic tier, with support for responses that include reasoning or conversational\\ncontent. Standard tier returns more consistent scores for differently worded responses\\nthat have the same meaning. It supports the same languages as Standard tier content\\nfilters. For more information, see Languages supported by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Standard tier requires that your\\nguardrail use cross-Region inference.\\nStandard tier for contextual grounding checks is available in a subset of the\\nAWS Regions that support safeguard tiers. For the list, see Supported Regions for safeguard tiers.\\n\\nIf you don't specify a tier, your guardrail uses Classic tier. **Both checks are optional guardrail policies.** Your guardrail has only content and sensitive-information filters, so neither is configured. Check how it treats optional policies.

**Contextual grounding check**
- It detects hallucinations by scoring each response for grounding (is it supported by a reference source?) and relevance (does it answer the query?). Both thresholds run from 0 to 0.99.
- It needs three inputs: a grounding source, a user query, and the content to guard. Typical uses are RAG, summarization, paraphrasing and question answering.
- Having no knowledge bases doesn't make the check inapplicable. You can supply the grounding source yourself through the Invoke, Converse or `ApplyGuardrail` APIs.
- It's mainly worth flagging if you have RAG-style or document-based apps. If your apps are pure free-form chat or classification, its absence matters much less.
- If you don't specify a tier, a guardrail uses the Classic tier. The Standard tier requires cross-Region inference.

**Automated Reasoning check**
- It validates model output against formal logic rules extracted from your own source documents, such as policies or rulebooks.
- It only applies if you've built an Automated Reasoning policy and attached its ARN to the guardrail, along with a confidence threshold. A guardrail with no policy ARNs has nothing to evaluate.
- It's relevant only if your use case has a rule set you need answers to follow, such as HR, compliance or eligibility logic. For most setups, absence isn't a misconfiguration.

For your setup, the likely reading is that neither check is configured. That's a coverage gap only if you have workloads that need hallucination detection or rule-based validation. It isn't a misconfiguration of the filters you do have.
